definition: Denigrate means to belittle someone or attack their reputation unfairly.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word denigrate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know denigrate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The old guidebooks denigrate the northern vineyards as fit only for vinegar, a judgment the medals have long since answered.
Belittle is far milder than denigrate — it shrinks its target ('cute little theory') but stays this side of dishonesty; to denigrate is to blacken a name with hints that are unfair or untrue.
Slander goes further than denigrate — denigration blackens a name with hints and unfairness; slander tells provable lies about it and can answer for them in court.

A smear is dirt thrown in public — headlines, campaign ads, posters on every pole — meant for the widest possible audience. Denigrate works far more quietly: the same reputation blackened in asides and hints, often behind the target's back.

Badmouth is the kitchen-table version: offhand griping about someone, endless but casual, with no plan behind it. To denigrate is deliberate work — belittling a person or attacking their reputation unfairly, each remark aimed where it will do harm.

Latin niger, "black," left almost nothing behind in everyday English — denigrate carries the root alone. Keep the picture instead of hunting for cousins: a reputation dipped in ink.
Denigrate means to belittle someone or attack their reputation unfairly.

The cliff collector sold her finds to the same museums that would not hire her, and for years their bulletins denigrated her in asides: a "dealer," a "local scavenger," a lucky amateur — each label dropped just where a curator's doubt could do the most damage.
The skeletons she pulled from the rock now anchor three national collections, several still wearing the little card that leaves her name off.
Denigrate is the exact word for those labels, because it means to belittle someone or attack their reputation unfairly — and the unfairness is baked in.
Honest criticism weighs the work and finds it wanting; denigration goes around the work to blacken the worker's name.
Denigrate says the attack was unfair — use it and you have taken the victim's side.

Inside this unit, mind the lanes: deride mocks to someone's face, demean lowers a person's dignity in how they are treated, deprecate talks a thing's worth down, and denigrate blackens a name, usually behind its back.
Smear is its tabloid twin.

denigrate: Slander goes further than denigrate — denigration blackens a name with hints and unfairness; slander tells provable lies about it and can answer for them in court.
Recruits visiting State always heard the same asides about its crosstown rival.
Coach Weller never attacked the other program in interviews.
Instead he would denigrate it quietly, player by player: a hint that its training was outdated, a suggestion that its graduates rarely started professionally.
The rival's methods filled coaching journals, and its alumni crowded league rosters.
For years the trick worked, because none of it was said where it could be checked.
Then a recruit posted the whole pitch online, sources and all, and the quiet campaign ended the only way it could — loudly.
